title: Redefining Synovial Pathotypes in Psoriatic Arthritis through Multi-Modal Histology and Machine Learning (The PSYNOVIUM Study)
authors: Hum, R. M.; Christofi, M.; Smith, S. L.; Tan, Y.; Shukla, R.; Marshall, L. M.; Smith, M.; Williams, A.; Orozco, G.; Viatte, S.; Buch, M.; Barton, A.; Ho, P.; Martin, P.
abstract: BackgroundSynovial inflammation in psoriatic arthritis (PsA) lacks a validated histological classification framework. Current approaches apply rheumatoid arthritis (RA) synovial pathotypes to PsA, which overlooks immunobiological differences between the diseases and limits the predictive power of tissue stratification. We aimed to define data-driven, PsA-specific synovial pathotypes to facilitate tissue-driven precision medicine. MethodsIn this cross-sectional study, ultrasound-guided synovial biopsies were obtained from 61 patients with PsA (n=22), seropositive RA (n=23), seronegative RA (n=10), and other inflammatory arthritides (n=6). Sections underwent multi-modal staining, including H&E, picrosirius red, and immunohisto-chemistry for CD3, CD20, CD68, CD138, and CD31. Whole-slide digital image analysis and automated pixel classifiers quantified cellular and stromal metrics. Unsupervised hierarchical clustering identified intrinsic PsA pathotypes, which were correlated with clinical disease activity, radiographic osteoarthritis (OA), and longitudinal treatment responses. FindingsWhile a subset of PsA patients shared an inflammatory signature with seropositive RA, unsupervised clustering of the PsA cohort revealed three distinct, novel pathotypes: Dense Myeloid (macrophage-driven), Fibro-Stromal (fibrosis and pauci-immune), and Angio-Lymphoid (hypervascular with significant CD138+ plasma cell infiltration). Pathotypes were independent of treatment and concurrent radiographic knee OA. The Fibro-Stromal pathotype correlated with significantly higher cutaneous psoriasis severity. Longitudinally, patients with the Fibro-Stromal pathotype exhibited a trend toward lower treatment response (44%) following standard interventions (methotrexate or TNF inhibitors) compared to the Dense Myeloid (50%) and Angio-Lymphoid (80%) pathotypes. InterpretationWe present the first computationally derived synovial pathotypes specific to PsA, revealing distinct plasma cell and fibrotic architectures not captured by RA-centric models. To enable clinical translation, we distilled these findings into a pragmatic, four-marker diagnostic decision tree (CD31, CD68, CD138, and picrosirius red) designed for routine histopathology workflows, providing a staging ground for biomarker-stratified clinical trials in PsA. FundingFunding from the NIHR Biomedical Research Centre: Manchester, Arthritis UK, the Wellcome Trust, Brit-PACT, the National Psoriasis Foundation, and the Medical Research Council. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSThe potential clinical utility of tissue-based patient stratification is well established in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), where baseline synovial pathotypes (lympho-myeloid, diffuse-myeloid, and pauciimmune) have guided targeted biologic therapy in landmark precision medicine trials. However, psoriatic arthritis (PsA) exhibits a fundamentally distinct synovial microenvironment, characterised by unique vascular architecture, altered stromal fibroblast phenotypes, and distinct immune infiltrates intertwined with the IL-23/IL-17 cytokine axis. Consequently, attempting to classify PsA synovial tissue using established RA-derived scoring systems risks misrepresenting intrinsic disease biology. There is currently no validated, disease-specific histological classification system for PsA, which forces therapeutic decision-making to rely on an empirical, trial-and-error approach rather than underlying target tissue pathobiology. Added value of this studyTo our knowledge, this is the first study to define data-driven, computationally derived synovial pathotypes entirely specific to PsA. By leveraging multi-modal digital pathology and unsupervised machine learning, we deconstructed the PsA synovium into three biologically distinct pathotypes: Dense Myeloid, Fibro-Stromal, and Angio-Lymphoid. We demonstrated that the highly inflammatory PsA microenvironment is distinctly driven by CD138+ plasma cells rather than the CD20+ B cells typically observed in RA. Furthermore, we identified a striking tissue-level divergence: patients with the highly fibrotic, pauci-immune Fibro-Stromal pathotype exhibited the most severe cutaneous psoriasis and demonstrated a trend toward higher failure rates on standard therapies, independent of concurrent osteoarthritis. Crucially, we translated these high-dimensional computational findings into a pragmatic, four-marker diagnostic decision tree (incorporating CD31, CD68, CD138, and picrosirius red). Implications of all the available evidenceThis study establishes that PsA synovial pathology requires a dedicated, disease-specific classification framework. The proposed diagnostic decision tree can be integrated into routine clinical histopathology workflows without the immediate need for advanced spatial or single-cell transcriptomics. Furthermore, the correlation between the Fibro-Stromal pathotype, severe skin disease, and poor joint response to standard therapies provides a biological rationale for stratifying this specific subgroup towards early IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor intervention alongside conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs. Ultimately, these novel PsA pathotypes provide the vital staging ground required to design and execute biomarker-stratified, tissue-driven clinical trials, paving the way for precision medicine in PsA.

infographic.key_insight: Machine-learning analysis identified three PsA-specific synovial tissue patterns: Dense Myeloid, Fibro-Stromal, and Angio-Lymphoid.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These tissue patterns could support future precision-medicine research, but their ability to guide treatment remains unvalidated.
method: Analyzed ultrasound-guided synovial biopsies using multi-modal staining and digital whole-slide imaging.
Used automated pixel classifiers to quantify cellular and stromal features.
Applied unsupervised hierarchical clustering to identify PsA pathotypes and explore clinical associations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 61 participants, including 22 with PsA, exploratory treatment-response rates were 44% for Fibro-Stromal, 50% for Dense Myeloid, and 80% for Angio-Lymphoid.
infographic.watch_item: The small PsA cohort and exploratory response trends require independent prospective validation before clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: Redefining Synovial Pathotypes in Psoriatic Arthritis through Multi-Modal Histology and Machine Learning (The PSYNOVIUM Study)

title: Applications of Fairness Training in Artificial Intelligence to Ophthalmic Disease Diagnosis using External Eye Photographs
authors: Kostin, V.; Yoon, S.-H.; Chen, J. S.; Baek, S.; Seid, J.; Quyang, N.; Li, E.; Li, E.; Shi, M.; Wang, M.
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR), age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and glaucoma are leading causes of preventable blindness, yet whether external eye photographs carry phenotypic information about posterior segment disease remains unclear, and methods to mitigate demographic disparities in such models are largely unexplored. We developed and evaluated deep learning and vision-language models for binary classification of vision-threatening DR (VTDR), advanced AMD, and glaucoma using 40,687 external eye photographs from 9,878 patients at Massachusetts Eye and Ear. Convolutional networks (WResNet, EfficientNet), a vision transformer (ViT), and a finetuned vision-language model (LLaVA) were assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with fairness across sex, race, and ethnicity quantified by the equity-scaled AUC (ES-AUC). Five fairness-training strategies were applied to the best models. LLaVA achieved the highest baseline AUC for VTDR (85{middle dot}4%, comparable to ViT 82{middle dot}6%); advanced AMD was similar across architectures (EfficientNet 86{middle dot}3%; LLaVA 84{middle dot}8%; ViT 84{middle dot}7%), whereas glaucoma was substantially worse (67-74%). Fairness training improved VTDR and AMD AUCs to 86{middle dot}3% and 85{middle dot}9% while partially mitigating demographic disparities. In summary, although AI models that rely on external eye photography to detect posterior segment disease may not yet be suitable for clinical deployment, the fairness methods demonstrated in this proof-of-concept study could be applied to other AI systems to decrease performance disparities and potentially improve model performance.

infographic.key_insight: AI detected signals of vision-threatening diabetic retinopathy and advanced AMD in external eye photographs, while fairness training partially reduced demographic performance disparities.
infographic.clinical_relevance: External eye photography may offer a way to assess posterior eye disease, but these proof-of-concept models are not yet suitable for clinical deployment.
method: Trained convolutional networks, a vision transformer, and a vision-language model to classify three eye diseases.
Evaluated discrimination using AUC and demographic fairness using equity-scaled AUC across sex, race, and ethnicity.
Applied five fairness-training strategies to the best-performing models.
infographic.evidence_signal: In 40,687 photographs from 9,878 patients at Massachusetts Eye and Ear, baseline AUC reached 85.4% for vision-threatening diabetic retinopathy and 86.3% for advanced AMD, versus 67–74% for glaucoma.
infographic.watch_item: Single-center evidence and remaining demographic disparities limit conclusions about generalizability and clinical readiness.
infographic.paper_title: Applications of Fairness Training in Artificial Intelligence to Ophthalmic Disease Diagnosis using External Eye Photographs

title: Agentic Pipeline for Large-Scale Clinical Data Queries in Enterprise Electronic Health Records
authors: Pawar, K.; Tavabi, N.; Kalepalli, A.; Kalepalli, N.; Blackmon, M.; Williamson, A.; Kiapour, A.
abstract: Using electronic health record (EHR) data to answer clinical research questions is challenging. It requires understanding the research question, finding relevant information across different sources, and combining that information to produce meaningful results. We developed an agentic large language model (LLM) pipeline that decomposes investigator-authored requests into source-specific tasks, generates and executes SQL on EHR, integrates structured and unstructured EHR evidence, and applies study-specific clinical note adjudication. We evaluated this workflow against data analyst-identified cohorts across 50 pediatric orthopedic clinical data query requests. Of these, 43 were included in manual-review-adjusted performance analyses. The median adjusted positive predictive value, sensitivity among patients identified by either approach, and corresponding F1 score were 0.93 (95% CI, 0.88-0.98), 0.92 (95% CI, 0.90-0.95) and 0.90 (95% CI, 0.87-0.94), respectively. These findings support the feasibility of translating natural-language research intent into executable, autonomous multi-stage EHR workflows.

infographic.key_insight: An agentic LLM pipeline translated natural-language research requests into multi-stage EHR queries, achieving a median adjusted F1 score of 0.90.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could help researchers identify study cohorts across structured records and clinical notes.
method: Decompose investigator requests into source-specific tasks.
Generate and execute SQL queries on EHR data.
Integrate structured and unstructured evidence with study-specific clinical note adjudication.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated against analyst-identified cohorts for 50 pediatric orthopedic requests, with 43 in manual-review-adjusted analyses: median PPV 0.93, sensitivity among patients identified by either approach 0.92, and F1 0.90.
infographic.watch_item: Sensitivity was measured only among patients identified by either approach, so patients missed by both were not captured by that metric.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic Pipeline for Large-Scale Clinical Data Queries in Enterprise Electronic Health Records

title: Benchmarking Large Language AI Models Against Human Doctors Using an Emergency Medicine Simulation Approach
authors: Shahabian, M.; Hadizadeh Esfahani, A.; Ahmadi, M.; Rajabzadeh, S.; Givechin Ghamsari, M. H.; Tabaraee, A.; Hejripour Rafsanjani, S. Z.
abstract: BackgroundProper adoption of AI in emergency medicine necessitate thorough and rigorous appraisal. Classic benchmarks, which rely heavily on basic question-and-answer formats, though dominating the benchmarking field of LLM usage in medicine, have proven inadequate in assessing the full spectrum of skills incumbent upon an agent in healthcare. MethodsWe propose an intricate benchmarking scheme in which the skill set required of an emergency physician is tested and quantified. Our benchmarking structure is 3-fold: skills such as history taking, diagnostic accuracy, treatment plan, and empathy are evaluated by an emergency medicine expert, while the same expertise is scored by an intern from the perspective of a patient, through what we call a simulated emergency room visit. A comprehensive written examination is also utilized to measure general emergency medicine knowledge. ResultsEight LLMs were benchmarked against each other and in contrast to nine emergency medical doctors. Our findings indicate that the AI models significantly outperformed human physicians across several key domains, including history taking, investigation, diagnostic accuracy, and treatment planning. Furthermore, the models demonstrated superior performance in comprehensibility, credibility, and empathy. When comparing AI models against each other, performance advantages were marginal during simulated emergency room visits and were mostly pronounced during the written examination. ConclusionAI models demonstrate a clear advantage over human physicians across a diverse range of emergency medicine competencies. The proposed benchmarking scheme provides a comprehensive metric for a thorough evaluation of medical skill set, furthering validation, adaptation, and utilization of AI in emergency medicine.

infographic.key_insight: In an emergency medicine simulation benchmark, eight LLMs outperformed nine physicians across several assessed clinical skills and patient-facing communication measures.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Simulation-based evaluation may help assess medical AI beyond question-answer tests, but these findings do not establish safety or effectiveness in real emergency care.
method: An emergency medicine expert assessed clinical skills during simulated emergency visits.
An intern acting as a patient rated patient-facing performance.
A written examination tested general emergency medicine knowledge.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports significant AI advantages in history taking, investigation, diagnostic accuracy, treatment planning, comprehensibility, credibility, and empathy, but provides no numerical effect sizes.
infographic.watch_item: The small physician comparator group and simulated setting limit generalizability to real-world emergency care.
infographic.paper_title: Benchmarking Large Language AI Models Against Human Doctors Using an Emergency Medicine Simulation Approach

title: Exploring Data Augmentation for Stroke Severity Prediction: How Generative AI Enhances EEG Signal Classification
authors: Sarkar, M. S. S.; Saon, M. T. H.; Basak, S.
abstract: In clinical datasets, data augmentation is often avoided because it can remove important unusual values, known as outliers, which are important for understanding diseases accurately. However, clinical EEG datasets often suffer from two key limitations: small sample sizes and class imbalance, which significantly reduce classification performance. To over-come these challenges, this study applies generative AI-based data augmentation techniques with a carefully designed hybrid pipeline that effectively enhances performance even on limited EEG data. Using EEG signals from 50 brain stroke patients [1], we investigate both traditional oversampling methods (SMOTE and ADASYN [2]) and advanced generative models, including WGAN and WGAN-GP. Our proposed pipeline involves pre-processing EEG recordings, extracting comprehensive statistical and frequency-domain features, applying feature reduction, and evaluating multiple machine learning classifiers. Experimental results show that the combination of SelectKBest feature selection, SVM classifier, and WGAN-GP augmentation achieves the highest classification accuracy of 72%, outperforming other methods. This work introduces a novel hybrid approach for EEG-based stroke severity classification, demonstrating that generative augmentation, when integrated properly, can significantly improve performance on small clinical datasets. To the best of our knowledge, this combination of techniques has not been explored before on any dataset, providing a solid foundation for future research in automated EEG-based stroke diagnosis.

infographic.key_insight: WGAN-GP augmentation combined with SelectKBest feature selection and an SVM achieved the highest reported accuracy of 72% for EEG-based stroke severity classification.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Generative augmentation may support research on stroke severity prediction when EEG datasets are small or imbalanced, but clinical utility remains unestablished.
method: Preprocess EEG signals and extract statistical and frequency-domain features.
Compare SMOTE, ADASYN, WGAN, and WGAN-GP augmentation.
Apply feature reduction and evaluate multiple machine learning classifiers.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using EEG data from 50 stroke patients, the study reported a best classification accuracy of 72%; the abstract does not specify validation design or uncertainty estimates.
infographic.watch_item: The small cohort and unspecified validation design leave generalizability uncertain; independent validation is needed before clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: Exploring Data Augmentation for Stroke Severity Prediction: How Generative AI Enhances EEG Signal Classification

title: Genomic Studies in Blood and Marrow Transplantation (GS-BMT): An NCI-CIBMTR genomic medicine initiative in hematopoietic cell transplantation
authors: Gadalla, S. M.; Lee, N.; Wu, X.; Pirsl, F.; Schmidt, G.; Rafati, M.; Hutchinson, A.; Vogt, A.; Hicks, B.; Liu, J.; Wang, J.; Gaddam, S.; Li, S.; Saber, W.; Chanock, S.; Kraft, P.; Savage, S. A.; Hong, H. G.; Spellman, S. R.
abstract: BackgroundGenomic studies in hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) are limited by sample sizes and targeted approaches. MethodsThe Genomic Studies in Blood and Marrow Transplantation (GS-BMT) project is a collaboration between the National Cancer Institute (NCI) and the CIBMTR(R) designed to investigate recipient and donor determinants of HCT outcomes. We are generating genome-wide SNP-array genotyping for all samples, and sequencing and methylation profiling for selected subsets. We report study design and cohort characteristics and present two proof-of-concept analyses: comparison of conventional and machine learning prediction of overall survival after HCT in 9,262 patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and assessment of inherited susceptibility to clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) among 19,750 HCT donors using polygenic scores (PGS). ResultsGS-BMT includes 30,718 donor-recipient pairs who received allogeneic HCT in the United States between 2000 and 2019. In AML, clinical variables alone provided modest prediction for post-transplant survival, with similar performance for Cox proportional hazards, random survival forest, and deep neural network survival models (C-index=0.63, 0.62, and 0.62, respectively). In donors, CHIP-PGS did not differ by age (p=0.76) but was modestly lower in unrelated vs. related donors (-0.06 standard deviation [SD]; p=0.002). In an illustrative analysis assuming risk of event increases by 50% or 80% per PGS-SD, the top 5.2% and 12.3% of the donors, respectively, would have at least twice the risk of a donor with the average PGS. ConclusionsGS-BMT establishes a large genomic platform aiming to improve individualized risk prediction, donor selection, and precision medicine in HCT.

infographic.key_insight: GS-BMT establishes a large transplant genomics platform, while initial AML analyses found no survival-prediction advantage for machine learning over a conventional Cox model using clinical variables alone.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The platform aims to support individualized transplant risk prediction and donor selection, but these initial findings do not establish clinical utility.
method: Assemble 30,718 donor–recipient pairs from U.S. allogeneic transplants performed in 2000–2019, with genome-wide genotyping and selected sequencing and methylation profiling.
Compare Cox, random survival forest, and deep neural network survival models in 9,262 patients with AML.
Assess inherited susceptibility to clonal hematopoiesis using polygenic scores in 19,750 donors.
infographic.evidence_signal: AML survival C-indices were 0.63 for Cox and 0.62 for both machine learning models; donor polygenic scores showed no age difference and were modestly lower in unrelated donors.
infographic.watch_item: The donor polygenic-score risk estimates were illustrative and assumption-based, not demonstrated predictions of observed clinical events.
infographic.paper_title: Genomic Studies in Blood and Marrow Transplantation (GS-BMT): An NCI-CIBMTR genomic medicine initiative in hematopoietic cell transplantation

title: Serum brain-derived tau distinguishes acute neurotrauma diagnoses
authors: Shi, R.; Svirsky, S. E.; Balogun, W. G.; Zeng, X.; Fedak, J. D.; Nafash, M.; Brodman, S. T.; Okonkwo, D. O.; Puccio, A. M.; Karikari, T. K.
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) and spinal cord injury (SCI) are two common forms of neurotrauma that can present with overlapping clinical features, complicating early diagnosis and management particularly in acute and mixed-trauma settings.1-3 Accurate and rapid biological differentiation remains an unmet need.4 We hypothesized that brain-derived tau (BD-tau), an ultrasensitive blood-based biomarker preferentially selective for tau protein originating from the brain, would distinguish TBI from SCI. In a multi-cohort assessment of 342 patients admitted to the neuro-intensive care unit (285 with TBI, 57 with SCI), and 22 controls, baseline serum BD-tau concentrations were markedly elevated in TBI compared with SCI, discriminating between the two populations with high accuracy (area under the curve [AUC]=0.91, 95%CI 0.87-0.96). In paired serum-cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples, serum BD-tau significantly outperformed CSF BD-tau for injury-type discrimination (AUC=0.95, 95%CI 0.89-0.99 vs. 0.80, 95%CI 0.71-0.89). Baseline serum BD-tau also showed superior discrimination of TBI from SCI compared with established blood biomarkers of neurotrauma, including neurofilament light chain, glial fibrillary acidic protein, and ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1 (AUC=0.82, 95%CI 0.76-0.88; vs. 0.53, 95%CI 0.43-0.63; 0.67, 95%CI 0.58-0.76; 0.71, 95%CI 0.64-0.79; all DeLong p<0.001). Longitudinally, serum BD-tau remained persistently elevated in TBI, but not SCI, for up to 144 hours post-injury, with distinct temporal trajectories between injury types. Together, these findings indicate that serum BD-tau enables rapid and minimally invasive differentiation of TBI from SCI and may support early clinical decision-making, triage, and enrollment into injury-specific therapeutic trials, highlighting the potential of circulating biomarkers to improve precision diagnostics in acute neurotrauma care.

infographic.key_insight: Serum brain-derived tau (BD-tau) distinguished traumatic brain injury (TBI) from spinal cord injury (SCI) with high accuracy in acute neurotrauma cohorts.
infographic.clinical_relevance: BD-tau could support injury-specific triage and trial enrollment, but its role in routine care requires further validation.
method: Assessed baseline serum BD-tau in 285 patients with TBI, 57 with SCI, and 22 controls.
Compared discrimination with paired cerebrospinal fluid samples and established blood biomarkers.
Tracked serum BD-tau trajectories for up to 144 hours after injury.
infographic.evidence_signal: Overall TBI-versus-SCI discrimination reached AUC 0.91 (95% CI 0.87–0.96); separate analyses favored serum over cerebrospinal fluid BD-tau and established blood biomarkers.
infographic.watch_item: Performance in these neuro-intensive care cohorts may not generalize to broader emergency populations or mixed TBI–SCI injuries.
infographic.paper_title: Serum brain-derived tau distinguishes acute neurotrauma diagnoses

title: Multi-Agent Generative Artificial Intelligence for Transfusion Reaction Feature Extraction
authors: Kumari, A.; Jacobs, J. W.; Dilly, L.; Anand, A.; Woo, J.; Lin, Y.; Shih, A. W.; Booth, G. S.; Raslan, I.; Relke, N.; Dubey, R.; Srivastava, S.; Abdulwahab, W.; Goel, R.; Raza, S.
abstract: BACKGROUNDMany transfusion reactions are not reported to hemovigilance systems, and the features needed to recognize them are often documented only in free-text clinical notes. We sought to develop and evaluate an open-source, multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline to extract transfusion reaction features defined by the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) Hemovigilance Module from clinical notes. METHODSWe curated 181 features from the NHSN protocol and developed a multi-stage pipeline that extracted features, their timing, and clinical details from free-text notes. Three open-weight large language models (Qwen 3.6-27B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Kimi K3) were applied to 50 notes from expert-written scenarios, published case reports, and MIMIC-IV discharge summaries. Two physicians independently evaluated every model output in a blinded interface. The primary analysis was restricted to feature occurrences with concordant physician assessments. RESULTSPhysicians agreed on 1,201 of 1,343 co-rated feature occurrences (89.4%; Krippendorffs 0.73). Precision was above 0.98 for all models. Sensitivity was 0.774 (95% CI 0.745-0.800) for Kimi K3, 0.636 (0.604-0.667) for GPT-OSS-120B, and 0.624 (0.593-0.655) for Qwen 3.6-27B, and specificity ranged from 0.952 to 0.991. Omissions accounted for more than 94% of false negatives. Timing and clinical details were judged supported or reasonable in more than 92% and 97% of assessments, respectively. Results were consistent across note sources and in analyses including discordant assessments. CONCLUSIONMulti-agent AI pipelines provide a feasible method for extracting transfusion reaction signals from clinical notes with high precision. Our work may have applications in active hemovigilance, reaction classification, and big data research.

infographic.key_insight: A multi-agent AI pipeline extracted transfusion reaction features from clinical notes with precision above 98%, but sensitivity varied from 62.4% to 77.4% across models.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support hemovigilance by identifying reaction-related signals in free-text notes, though clinical deployment was not evaluated.
method: Curated 181 features from the NHSN Hemovigilance Module protocol.
Tested three open-weight language models in a multi-stage pipeline extracting features, timing, and clinical details.
Two physicians independently reviewed outputs from 50 notes in a blinded interface.
infographic.evidence_signal: Physicians agreed on 1,201 of 1,343 co-rated feature occurrences (89.4%); among concordant assessments, Kimi K3 had the highest sensitivity at 77.4% (95% CI 74.5–80.0%).
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation covered only 50 notes, and omissions accounted for over 94% of false negatives, warranting broader validation before operational use.
infographic.paper_title: Multi-Agent Generative Artificial Intelligence for Transfusion Reaction Feature Extraction

title: Development of a deep learning model for glomerulus detection and segmentation in kidney histopathology images
authors: Tosaki, T.; Sasaki, T.; Okabayashi, Y.; Haruhara, K.; Okabe, M.; Tsuboi, N.; Yokoo, T.
abstract: BackgroundEstimation of nephron number, an indicator of renal reserve, requires quantitative assessment of glomerular number and size in kidney biopsy specimens. We aimed to develop an automated system for quantitative measurement of glomerular areas from clinical kidney biopsy images, across diverse kidney diseases. MethodsWe developed a two-stage deep learning system combining Faster R-CNN for glomerular detection in whole-slide images (WSIs) and DeepLabV3+ for segmentation. Of 114 kidney biopsies (228 WSIs), 104 were used for model development and 10 for independent final evaluation. Agreement was assessed using the F1-score for detection, the Dice coefficient for segmentation, and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for glomerular area measurement. Analysis was performed at 40x total magnification (2.331 m/pixel) and validated against 400x images. ResultsIn the independent evaluation set, the artificial intelligence (AI) model achieved a mean F1-score of 0.851 for detection, compared with 0.888 among experts. For segmentation, the Dice coefficient was 0.959 {+/-} 0.011 and the per-pair ICC (2,1) for area measurement was 0.989 {+/-} 0.009; both were comparable to inter-expert agreement. Bland-Altman analysis showed a mean bias of -344 m{superscript 2} (95% limits of agreement, -1904 to 1216 m{superscript 2}) between 40x and 400x measurements. ConclusionThe two-stage model achieved glomerular segmentation and area measurement comparable to expert agreement in independent clinical data, with detection performance approaching inter-expert agreement, and provided reliable measurements at low magnification. This automated approach may facilitate large-scale quantitative kidney pathology and nephron number estimation from clinical kidney biopsies.

infographic.key_insight: A two-stage AI system measured glomerular areas with expert-comparable agreement, while detection approached inter-expert performance.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Automated glomerular measurement could support large-scale quantitative kidney pathology and research on nephron number estimation.
method: Faster R-CNN detected glomeruli in whole-slide kidney biopsy images.
DeepLabV3+ segmented detected glomeruli for area measurement.
Low-magnification measurements at 40× were compared with 400× measurements.
infographic.evidence_signal: Of 114 biopsies, 104 supported development and 10 independent final evaluation; AI achieved detection F1 0.851 versus expert agreement of 0.888, segmentation Dice 0.959, and area-measurement ICC 0.989.
infographic.watch_item: The independent evaluation included only 10 biopsies; broader validation is needed before routine clinical implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Development of a deep learning model for glomerulus detection and segmentation in kidney histopathology images

title: LLM Embeddings Complement Theory-Driven Language Features and Cognitive Scores for APOE4 and Aβ Prediction
authors: Zadok, M.; Calderon, N.; Wald, Y.; Rein, N.; Ganmore, I.; Lesman-Segev, O.; Almog, G.; Shamir, T.; Ackler, R.; Leviner, S. Y.; Noimark, G.; Levy, G.; Mueller, K. D.; Ravona Springer, R.; Schnaider Beeri, M.; Reichart, R.
abstract: Spontaneous language offers a scalable, noninvasive approach for identifying biological indicators of preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD). We examined prediction of APOE4 carrier status and cerebral amyloid-beta burden using Cookie Theft picture descriptions from two cohorts of Hebrew- and English-speaking participants (IRAP, N=134; WRAP, N=1,541). Amyloid-beta burden was classified using lowest-quartile, median, and highest-quartile cutoffs, capturing accumulation below conventional amyloid-positivity thresholds. We compared embeddings from pretrained large language models (LLMs) with standard cognitive test scores, reflecting conventional clinical assessment, and theory-driven linguistic features, reflecting traditional language analysis. Embedding-based models achieved the highest F1 scores among constituent models in five of eight tasks involving APOE4 status and global amyloid-beta burden. High prediction disagreement suggested complementary signals across approaches. An any-positive ensemble significantly outperformed every constituent model and a prior-informed random baseline across all eight tasks, and significantly outperformed all constituent models in 21 of 24 regional amyloid-beta tasks. These findings highlight the complementarity of LLM-based, theory-driven, and cognitive measures for predicting AD-related genetic risk and amyloid pathology, and support further investigation of their potential for early screening approaches.

infographic.key_insight: LLM embeddings complemented theory-driven language features and cognitive scores, with an any-positive ensemble improving prediction of APOE4 carrier status and amyloid-beta burden.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Picture-description language may support future noninvasive screening research for Alzheimer’s-related risk and pathology, but clinical utility remains unestablished.
method: Analyzed Cookie Theft picture descriptions from Hebrew- and English-speaking cohorts.
Compared pretrained LLM embeddings, theory-driven linguistic features, and cognitive test scores.
Combined predictions using an any-positive ensemble and evaluated multiple amyloid-beta cutoffs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across IRAP (N=134) and WRAP (N=1,541), the ensemble significantly outperformed every constituent model and a prior-informed random baseline on all 8 APOE4/global amyloid-beta tasks, and all constituent models on 21 of 24 regional amyloid-beta tasks.
infographic.watch_item: An any-positive ensemble may increase false positives; specificity and prospective clinical performance require validation before screening use.
infographic.paper_title: LLM Embeddings Complement Theory-Driven Language Features and Cognitive Scores for APOE4 and Aβ Prediction

title: Plasma phosphorylated tau species across neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular diseases: An ONDRI study
authors: Sanchez, E.; Connon, P.; Pasternak, M.; Abrahao, A.; Keith, J.; Dilliott, A. A.; Baril, A.-A.; Frank, A.; Lang, A. E.; Pollock, B. G.; Marras, C.; Fischer, C. E.; Seitz, D.; Dowlatshahi, D.; Grimes, D. A.; Tang-Wai, D. F.; Sahlas, D. J.; Rogaeva, E.; Finger, E.; Tan, K.; Binns, M. A.; Tartaglia, M. C.; Borrie, M.; Freedman, M.; Goncalves, R. A.; Swartz, R. H.; Hegele, R. A.; Dixon, R. A.; Mirza, S. S.; Farhan, S. M. K.; Black, S. E.; Kumar, S.; Pasternak, S. H.; Rajji, T. K.; Steeves, T.; Swardfager, W.; Zetterberg, H.; Kvartsberg, H.; Munoz, D. P.; Zinman, L.; Strong, M. J.; Masellis, M.
abstract: Elevated plasma phosphorylated tau (p-tau) species are proposed as specific biomarkers of Alzheimers disease (AD) pathology but have also been reported in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Their profile across neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular diseases, as well as their discriminatory value when combined with other plasma biomarkers, remain uncertain. We studied 551 participants (ages 40.1 to 87.1 years; 207 women), comprising 506 patients from the Ontario Neurodegenerative Disease Research Initiative (ONDRI) multi-site cohort and 45 amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}) PET-negative cognitively unimpaired controls from the Brain-Eye Amyloid Memory study. Ten diagnostic groups were studied: mild cognitive impairment (MCI), AD, Parkinsons disease subdivided into cognitively unimpaired (CU), MCI, and dementia, frontotemporal dementia (FTD), cerebrovascular disease (CVD) subdivided into cognitively unimpaired (CU) and cognitively impaired (CI), ALS, and the control group. Baseline visit plasma measurements included p-tau217, p-tau181, A{beta}42/40, neurofilament light chain (NfL), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). Cross-sectional analyses compared biomarker levels as well as p-tau217-based inference of amyloid positivity status across diagnostic groups. Receiver operating characteristic-area under the curve (ROC-AUC) analyses ascertained the discriminatory capacity of these biomarkers and ratio combinations. Within the ALS group, baseline biomarker measures were also tested for association against baseline clinical features as well as longitudinal measures of neuropsychological change. P-tau217, p-tau181, GFAP, and NfL differed across groups (all P < 0.001). Compared to controls, p-tau217 was elevated in AD and ALS, p-tau181 and GFAP only in AD, and NfL in ALS and FTD. Inferred amyloid-{beta} positivity was more probable in MCI, AD, ALS, and cognitively impaired CVD groups compared to controls (all P < 0.05). The p-tau217 to NfL ratio discriminated ALS from AD with an ROC-AUC of 0.92 (95% CI 0.85-0.97) compared to p-tau217 alone at 0.65 (95% CI 0.52-0.76). No ALS clinical or longitudinal association survived correction for multiple comparisons. Elevated p-tau217 and inferred amyloid-{beta} positivity in ALS provide further evidence that the assay signal is not necessarily specific for AD pathology. However, the use of p-tau217 in combination with NfL provides improved discriminatory power between ALS and AD, supporting the use of plasma biomarker combinations rather than sole reliance on individual plasma biomarkers. Inferred amyloid-{beta} positivity in cognitively impaired CVD may indicate AD and/or cerebral amyloid angiopathy co-pathology. Currently available plasma biomarkers should therefore be used as diagnostic complements and interpreted within clinical context rather than as standalone molecular diagnoses.

infographic.key_insight: Plasma p-tau217 was elevated in both Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and ALS, but its ratio to neurofilament light chain (NfL) distinguished the two better than p-tau217 alone.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These findings suggest that elevated p-tau217 alone may not be specific to AD and that combining biomarkers could improve disease discrimination.
method: Measured baseline plasma p-tau217, p-tau181, Aβ42/40, NfL, and GFAP in 551 participants across 10 diagnostic groups.
Compared biomarker levels and p-tau217-inferred amyloid positivity across groups.
Evaluated discrimination using ROC-AUC and explored clinical and longitudinal cognitive associations in ALS.
infographic.evidence_signal: The p-tau217/NfL ratio distinguished ALS from AD with an AUC of 0.92 (95% CI 0.85–0.97), versus 0.65 (0.52–0.76) for p-tau217 alone.
infographic.watch_item: The reported discrimination comes from a primarily cross-sectional cohort analysis and requires independent validation before clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: Plasma phosphorylated tau species across neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular diseases: An ONDRI study

title: Randomized Trial Protocol: Head-to-Head Comparison of Two Ambient Artificial Intelligence Documentation Tools on Clinician Usability
authors: Chin, A. T.; Leung, K.; Vangala, S.; Woo, H.; Kingsley, T.; Sandhu, A.; Jalalian, L.; Cheng, E. M.; Mafi, J. N.; Lukac, P. J.
abstract: BackgroundAmbient AI documentation reduces documentation burden and electronic health record (EHR) time for ambulatory clinicians. Newer features also queue orders and offer some level of coding support for clinician review. This study compares two commercial products deployed at UCLA Health. ObjectiveTo compare Nabla and Epic Systems, Inc.s ambient AI solution among ambulatory clinicians at UCLA Health on usability, documentation burden, perceived note quality, adoption, EHR time and productivity, clinician-reported experience with order queueing and coding support, coding and billing patterns and integrity, work productivity, and patient-reported communication experience. MethodsTwo-arm parallel-group randomized trial, 1:1, among 374 ambulatory clinicians at a single academic health system who hold an active license for a standalone ambient application (Nabla). Randomization is covariate-constrained where cohort size permits, balancing age, sex, half-day clinic sessions, specialty group, and baseline System Usability Scale (SUS) score. Intervention runs 11/9/2026 to 1/17/2027, with the first four weeks as lead-in. The primary outcome is SUS score at follow-up, compared between arms. Analysis is by intention-to-treat using mixed-effects models. Ethics and disseminationDetermined exempt by the UCLA Institutional Review Board (IRB-26-2147). Survey completion indicates consent. No patient-level data are collected. Findings will directly inform operational decision making and will be published regardless of direction.

infographic.key_insight: This randomized trial protocol will compare Nabla with Epic’s ambient AI documentation solution; no comparative results are reported yet.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The study could inform health-system decisions about ambient AI usability, documentation workflows, and clinician experience.
method: Randomize 374 UCLA Health ambulatory clinicians with active Nabla licenses 1:1 to two parallel arms.
Run November 9, 2026–January 17, 2027, including a four-week lead-in.
Compare follow-up System Usability Scale scores using intention-to-treat mixed-effects models.
infographic.evidence_signal: The planned primary endpoint is clinician-rated usability, with additional evaluation of documentation burden, EHR time, adoption, coding patterns, and patient-reported communication.
infographic.watch_item: A single-system sample of clinicians already licensed for Nabla may limit generalizability to other settings or first-time users.

title: Towards the Virtual Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Patient: Inferring Cortical Excitability through Whole-Brain Dynamical Modeling
authors: Angiolelli, M.; Demuru, M.; Lopez, E. T.; Hashemi, M.; Ziaeemehr, A.; Rabuffo, G.; Trojsi, F.; Granata, C.; Tafuri, D.; De Luca, M.; Gallo, E.; Jirsa, V.; Depannemaecker, D.; Sorrentino, P.
abstract: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is increasingly recognized as a multisystem neurodegenerative disorder in which motor-neuron degeneration is accompanied by widespread alterations in cortical dynamics. Hyperexcitability is widespread across the brain, although more predominantly in motor and premotor areas. Yet, how local excitability imbalance shapes distributed whole-brain dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we combined source-reconstructed resting-state magnetoencephalography data, tractography-informed whole-brain modeling, and simulation-based inference to investigate whether ALS-related alterations in large-scale brain dynamics can be mechanistically explained by changes in cortical excitability. First, we characterized empirical brain dynamics using neuronal avalanche transition matrices (ATMs) on source-reconstructed magnetoencephalography data. These analyses revealed significant alterations in ALS patients relative to healthy controls. To interpret these changes mechanistically, we employed a reduced Wong-Wang whole-brain model in which local recurrent excitation modulates emergent large-scale neural dynamics. The model showed that increasing recurrent excitation uniformly across the brain produced changes in avalanche-derived features that were directionally consistent with the empirical alterations observed in ALS patients. Then, using simulation-based inference, we jointly estimated recurrent excitation and global coupling from individual empirical feature vectors. ALS patients exhibited higher inferred recurrent excitation than controls. A regional extension of the model, distinguishing motor and frontal from non-frontal regions, revealed more pronounced hyperexcitability in motor-frontal regions. Together, these findings support enhanced excitability as a candidate mechanism contributing to altered large-scale avalanche propagation in ALS. By integrating empirical brain dynamics with probabilistic model inversion, this framework provides individual-level mechanistic descriptors of disease-related brain activity and motivates further investigation of regional excitability alterations and their clinical relevance.

infographic.key_insight: Whole-brain modeling inferred higher cortical excitability in ALS, especially in motor-frontal regions, as a candidate mechanism for altered brain-wide activity propagation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework offers individual-level research descriptors of ALS-related brain dynamics, but their clinical relevance remains unvalidated.
method: Characterized neuronal avalanche transitions in source-reconstructed resting-state magnetoencephalography.
Used tractography-informed reduced Wong–Wang models to simulate whole-brain dynamics.
Applied simulation-based inference to estimate recurrent excitation and global coupling.
infographic.evidence_signal: ALS patients showed significant avalanche-transition alterations versus healthy controls and higher model-inferred recurrent excitation; simulated excitation increases produced directionally consistent changes.
infographic.watch_item: Excitability estimates are model-dependent rather than direct measurements, and the abstract does not report sample size or independent clinical validation.
infographic.paper_title: Towards the Virtual Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Patient: Inferring Cortical Excitability through Whole-Brain Dynamical Modeling

title: Examining the Clinical Utility of Deep Learning Models for Perivascular Space Segmentation in Alzheimer's Disease
authors: Tang, S.; Younes, K.; Penukonda, E.; Hausle, I.; Thropp, P.; Lupo, J. M.; Tosun, D.
abstract: Open-source deep learning models promise scalable quantification of MRI-visible perivascular spaces (PVS), an emerging marker of glymphatic dysfunction in Alzheimers disease (AD). Whether these models remain valid when applied to heterogeneous AD cohorts and preserve ground-truth derived biological associations has not been established. We benchmarked five open-source nnU-Net-based PVS segmentation models (nnU-Net T1, nnU-Net T1+FLAIR, mcPVS-Net, MedNet-PVS, ADNI-PVS-Net) against manual labels in 60 multi-site ADNI-3 participants balanced across cognitively unimpaired, mild cognitive impairment, and AD dementia, and in 12 publicly available scans from the VAscular Lesions Detection and segmentatiOn challenge (VALDO) challenge. We evaluated overall, voxel, object, and lesion-wise Dice; stratified performance by region, diagnosis, scanner, PVS severity, and white matter hyperintensity (WMH) burden; and tested whether model-derived PVS burden reproduced ground-truth derived associations with AD-related biomarkers. Despite high internal performance, all models showed a specialist-generalist trade-off: the AD-trained ADNI-PVS-Net achieved highest internal performance (overall Dice = 0.58{+/-}0.14) but degraded most externally (Dice [≤] 0.11), while MedNet-PVS and mcPVS-Net generalized externally (Dice 0.27-0.30) but systematically misestimated PVS burden. Models were relatively robust across scanner and diagnosis but inconsistent across PVS severity, and some misclassified up to 32% of WMH as PVS. Notably, only AD-trained models reproduced the expected PVS-amyloid biomarker relationship; other models returned a null result, despite comparable or superior Dice scores. These findings show that internal segmentation accuracy and external generalizability alone do not guarantee downstream inferential validity. Careful model selection and cohort-specific validation against manual labels should precede clinical inference in AD.

infographic.key_insight: High PVS segmentation accuracy did not guarantee valid Alzheimer’s biomarker associations; only AD-trained models reproduced the expected PVS–amyloid relationship.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Automated PVS measurements may support Alzheimer’s research, but require cohort-specific validation before clinical inference.
method: Benchmarked five open-source nnU-Net-based models against manual PVS labels.
Evaluated segmentation across regions, diagnoses, scanners, PVS severity, and white matter hyperintensity burden.
Tested whether model-derived PVS burden preserved manual-label associations with AD biomarkers.
infographic.evidence_signal: Testing included 60 multi-site ADNI-3 participants and 12 external VALDO scans; ADNI-PVS-Net achieved internal Dice of 0.58 ± 0.14 but external Dice ≤0.11.
infographic.watch_item: External testing was limited to 12 scans, and some models misclassified up to 32% of white matter hyperintensities as PVS.
infographic.paper_title: Examining the Clinical Utility of Deep Learning Models for Perivascular Space Segmentation in Alzheimer's Disease

title: Large Language Models to Label CT Radiology Reports for Incidental Findings Found in Lung Cancer Screening: A Comparative Analysis
authors: van der Graaf, F.; Antonissen, N.; Scholten, E. T.; Schalkx, H.; Prokop, M.; Jacobs, C.
abstract: ObjectiveTo compare LLM and prompting strategies for labeling Specific Incidental Findings (SIFs) occurring during lung cancer screening, in radiology reports. Materials and MethodsIn this retrospective study, 300 CT reports from a Dutch academic hospital were included between 19th March 2003 and 28th December 2020. GPT-5, GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-3.1-8B-INST, MedGemma-4B-IT, a keyword-based search method, and a radiologist labelled the reports for the presence or absence of nine SIFs. The radiologists scores were the reference standard. Each LLM was evaluated with four different prompting strategies: two without Chain-of-Thought (CoT), and two with CoT (one zero shot, one few shot). The automated labelling methods were evaluated against the radiologist primarily using Cohens Kappa, and additionally sensitivity, specificity, and F1 scores. ResultsGPT-5 achieved substantial or almost perfect agreement for seven out of nine SIFs: aortic valve disease, bronchiectasis, consolidation, coronary artery calcification, emphysema, abnormality in mediastinal lymph nodes, and thyroid abnormalities, with Cohen {kappa} values of 0.81 (0.70, 0.93), 0.97 (0.93, 1.00), 0.71 (0.62, 0.82), 0.92 (0.87, 0.96), 0.91 (0.84, 0.97), 0.71 (0.62, 0.80), and 0.92 (0.86, 0.98) respectively. For the remaining two SIFs, moderate LLM agreement was obtained with MedGemma-4B-IT and with GPT-4-Turbo with Cohen {kappa} values of 0.48 (0.40, 0.60), 0.42 (0.31, 0.58) for interstitial lung abnormalities and mediastinal mass respectively. The highest agreement was obtained with the non-CoT prompt strategies for most SIFs. ConclusionThis study demonstrated that LLMs can automatically label radiology reports with agreement ranging from almost perfect to moderate, but not one LLM - prompt combination achieved the highest agreement across all SIFs.

infographic.key_insight: GPT-5 achieved substantial or almost perfect agreement with radiologist labels for 7 of 9 incidental findings, but no model–prompt combination performed best across all findings.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Automated labeling could support research and quality-review workflows for incidental findings documented in lung cancer screening CT reports.
method: Retrospective analysis of 300 CT reports from one Dutch academic hospital, dated 2003–2020.
Compared four LLMs using four prompting strategies each, plus keyword-based search.
Evaluated against radiologist labels using Cohen’s kappa, sensitivity, specificity, and F1.
infographic.evidence_signal: GPT-5’s kappa ranged from 0.71–0.97 for seven findings; the best reported agreement for interstitial lung abnormalities and mediastinal mass was moderate (0.48 and 0.42, respectively).
infographic.watch_item: Single-center, report-level evaluation does not establish generalizability or accuracy for detecting findings directly on CT images.
infographic.paper_title: Large Language Models to Label CT Radiology Reports for Incidental Findings Found in Lung Cancer Screening: A Comparative Analysis

title: LungAI: An AI Biomarker that Refines Lung-RADS v2022 Triage of Screen-Detected Pulmonary Nodules
authors: Suri, H.; Keselman, Y.; Legel, L.; Govette, J.; Mullen, B.; Choradia, N.; Sartawi, T.; Abtin, F.; Moghanaki, D.; Thomson, C. C.; Yankelevitz, D. F.; Ahuja, Y.
abstract: BackgroundThe Lung-RADS algorithm standardizes the management of screen-detected pulmonary nodules, but its risk assessment is driven chiefly by nodule size and attenuation. This misallocates a meaningful fraction of patients: a nontrivial share of small malignancies receive 12-month surveillance while large benign nodules proceed to invasive workup. Artificial intelligence (AI) may supply risk information independent of the imaging features Lung-RADS already uses. MethodsWe validated LungAI, an investigational deep learning nodule malignancy classifier not yet cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), on the held-out NLST test partition of Ardila et al. (2,747 low-dose CT examinations from 1,244 patients with [≥]1 solid or part-solid 4-30 mm nodule; 89 pathologically confirmed cancers, prevalence 3.2%). We compared discrimination against Sybil, mean nodule diameter, and estimated nodule volume. A board-certified radiologist assigned Lung-RADS v2022 categories to a positives-enriched random subset (226 eligible examinations; 78 cancers), projected to the full cohort by contingency weighting. A per-category reclassification algorithm shifted patients along the existing Lung-RADS management ladder using a-priori score cutpoints. We evaluated a separately locked follow-up configuration on examinations with a prior scan. ResultsLungAI achieved AUROC 0.92 (95% CI 0.88-0.95) and AUPRC 0.47 (0.35-0.61), outperforming Sybil ({Delta}AUROC 0.07; {Delta}AUPRC 0.18), diameter ({Delta}AUROC 0.14; {Delta}AUPRC 0.34), and volume ({Delta}AUROC 0.14; {Delta}AUPRC 0.38; all P<0.001). Against Lung-RADS v2022 scored ordinally on the weighted annotated subset, LungAI improved AUPRC ({Delta}AUPRC 0.31, P=0.003) but not AUROC ({Delta}AUROC 0.03, P=0.20). LungAI added discriminative information independent of diameter (likelihood-ratio {chi}2=161, P<10-36; {Delta}AUROC 0.10) and, on follow-up examinations, independent of delta diameter, volume doubling time, and new-nodule status ({chi}2=79, P<10-18). Integrated with Lung-RADS, LungAI reduced cancers on the slowest (12-month rescan) pathway by 46% (3.1[->]1.6 per 1,000 examinations) and benign biopsy referrals by 20% (32.7[->]26.2 per 1,000 examinations) at approximately unchanged total biopsy volume (51.0[->]50.1 per 1,000). Assuming full adherence to recommended follow-up, the combined approach yielded 25 months of net diagnostic lead time, an estimated net cost saving of [~]$2,200, and 6.5 fewer benign biopsies per 1,000 examinations; accounting for published adherence rates, it yielded 1.6 additional cancer diagnoses within 1 year per 1,000 examinations. ConclusionsLungAI contributes malignancy-risk information orthogonal to the size- and growth-based features underlying Lung-RADS and improves the allocation of screening patients across the existing management spectrum while potentially decreasing invasive procedures for benign lesions. Multi-site, multi-geography validation is required to demonstrate practical generalizability.

infographic.key_insight: Integrating LungAI with Lung-RADS v2022 reduced cancers assigned to 12-month surveillance by 46% and benign biopsy referrals by 20% in the study analysis.
infographic.clinical_relevance: AI-derived nodule risk could help refine screening triage beyond size-based assessment, but improved patient outcomes remain unproven.
method: Validated LungAI on 2,747 held-out NLST CT examinations from 1,244 patients, including 89 cancers.
Compared performance with Sybil, nodule diameter, volume, and radiologist-assigned Lung-RADS v2022.
Applied prespecified AI score cutpoints to reclassify Lung-RADS pathways; separately evaluated a locked follow-up configuration.
infographic.evidence_signal: LungAI achieved AUROC 0.92 (95% CI 0.88–0.95); versus Lung-RADS on a weighted annotated subset, AUPRC improved significantly but AUROC did not.
infographic.watch_item: LungAI is investigational and not FDA-cleared; triage estimates relied on a weighted, cancer-enriched subset rather than prospective clinical deployment.
infographic.paper_title: LungAI: An AI Biomarker that Refines Lung-RADS v2022 Triage of Screen-Detected Pulmonary Nodules

title: Room-Aware Transformer for Activities of Daily Living Recognition in Adults with Mild Neurocognitive Disorder Using Ambient Sensors: Development and Evaluation Study
authors: Abdalnabi, N.; Addepalli, V. r.; Roessler, A.; Kiselica, A.; Kummerfeld, E.; Sarker, S.; Rao, P.; Lee, K.
abstract: AO_SCPLOWBSTRACTC_SCPLOWO_ST_ABSBackgroundC_ST_ABSUnobtrusive recognition of activities of daily living (ADLs) from ambient sensors may support longitudinal assessment of everyday functioning in adults with mild neurocognitive disorder (mild NCD). However, real-world activity recognition is complicated by heterogeneous home layouts, sensor configurations, routines, and class distributions. ObjectiveThis study evaluated whether a room-aware Transformer that preserves location-specific sensor structure improves participant-level ADL recognition relative to a global Transformer and a stacked unidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM) network. MethodsFollowing pilot feasibility testing with two adult volunteers, we analyzed five homes of adults with mild NCD, comprising 92,765 minute-level observations across 67 annotated home-days. Motion, temperature, illuminance, humidity, and door-contact data were aligned to participant activity logs. The original labels were harmonized into eight categories. Models were developed separately for each home using 10-, 30-, and 60-minute windows. Complete calendar days were assigned to mutually exclusive training, validation, and chronological test sets, and no sequence crossed a day or partition boundary. The same partitions and evaluation procedures were used for all three architectures. Performance was assessed on held-out test days using accuracy, per-class F1 score, and micro- and macro-averaged one-versus-rest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). ResultsThe room-aware Transformer achieved the highest or tied accuracy in 9 of 15 home-window comparisons. Its accuracy ranged from 0.27 to 0.57, micro-AUC from 0.57 to 0.82, and macro-AUC from 0.54 to 0.78. Across the 15 settings, mean accuracy was similar for the room-aware and global Transformers and higher than for the LSTM. Mean micro-AUC and macro-AUC were marginally higher for the global Transformer than for the room-aware Transformer. The room-aware model showed its clearest gains in selected contexts, including Homes C and E at 10 minutes and Home A at 60 minutes, but no architecture or temporal window was uniformly optimal. Sleep/Rest was the most consistently recognized activity, whereas low-support activities frequently had low F1 scores despite moderate or high AUC values. ConclusionsRoom-specific feature processing provided context-dependent gains in participant-level ADL classification, particularly for accuracy in several home-window settings. The marked variation across homes, activities, and temporal windows supports personalized model development, class-sensitive evaluation, and validation in larger and more diverse residential samples before clinical use.

infographic.key_insight: A room-aware Transformer achieved the highest or tied activity-recognition accuracy in 9 of 15 home-window comparisons, but no model was uniformly best.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Ambient-sensor activity recognition may support longitudinal assessment of everyday functioning in adults with mild neurocognitive disorder, though clinical utility remains unestablished.
method: Aligned motion, environmental, and door-contact sensor data with activity logs harmonized into eight categories.
Compared room-aware and global Transformers with a stacked LSTM, training models separately for each home.
Evaluated 10-, 30-, and 60-minute windows using day-separated training, validation, and chronological test sets.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five homes, 92,765 minute-level observations and 67 annotated home-days, room-aware test accuracy ranged from 0.27 to 0.57, with micro-AUC of 0.57–0.82 and macro-AUC of 0.54–0.78.
infographic.watch_item: The small, home-specific evaluation leaves generalization to new residents, layouts, and sensor configurations uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Room-Aware Transformer for Activities of Daily Living Recognition in Adults with Mild Neurocognitive Disorder Using Ambient Sensors: Development and Evaluation Study

title: Detection of early-stage cancer using similarity-based classification of cell-free DNA fragmentation patterns
authors: Wood, D. E.; Ballew, B. J.; Roy, J.
abstract: Current cancer screening efforts face the dual problems of low patient adherence and a lack of available tests for many cancers, which motivates the development of less invasive multi-cancer early detection strategies. Such strategies will likely involve the use of liquid biopsies, which can analyze biomarkers found in blood for the presence of cancer. We introduce Blackjack, a new detection approach that focuses on the fragmentation patterns of plasma-derived cell-free DNA (cfDNA). Blackjack characterizes a persons cfDNA fragmentation sites with a position probability matrix (PPM) that encodes information about the sequence context of the sites. For classification, Blackjack computes two features that represent the similarity of an individuals PPM to those of known healthy and cancer cohorts. With these two features, Blackjack then uses logistic regression to classify a new sample as being from a healthy individual or a person with cancer. In cross-validation experiments using two external whole genome sequencing datasets, Blackjack showed high performance, achieving a minimum area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.993 and minimum sensitivity (Sn) of 91.8% (at 98% specificity). This high performance was also present for stage I (AUC 0.991, Sn 89.8%) and stage II cancers (AUC 0.993, Sn 90.2%), and across eight different cancers (minimum AUC 0.985, minimum Sn 80.0%). We demonstrate that Blackjacks accuracy is stable at low simulated sequencing depths ([~]0.24x), and that tissue of origin prediction using Blackjacks similarity measures is high (minimum 82% accuracy of the top two predicted tissues). Our findings show that cfDNA fragmentation site contexts have valuable signals for early cancer detection, and that developing diagnostics with machine learning can benefit from a focus on having a small number of informative features.

infographic.key_insight: Blackjack uses two similarity-based features from cell-free DNA fragmentation patterns to distinguish cancer from healthy samples, including early-stage cancers.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support minimally invasive multi-cancer detection through blood testing, but clinical screening utility remains unproven.
method: Encode DNA sequence context around fragmentation sites in a position probability matrix.
Measure similarity to matrices from healthy and cancer reference cohorts.
Use the two similarity features in logistic regression.
infographic.evidence_signal: Cross-validation on two external whole-genome sequencing datasets yielded a minimum AUC of 0.993 and sensitivity of 91.8% at 98% specificity; stage I sensitivity was 89.8%.
infographic.watch_item: Cross-validation results require prospective validation in representative screening populations to establish real-world performance.
infographic.paper_title: Detection of early-stage cancer using similarity-based classification of cell-free DNA fragmentation patterns

title: Browser-Based Video Supports Scalable Computer Vision Analysis for Open Surgical Skill Assessment
authors: Khan, A.; Kulkarni, S.; Lai, S.-L.; Wang, X.; Farber, I.; Kugener, G.; Pal, A.; Volpi, S.; Zohar, O.; Chen, C.-S.; Yeung-Levy, S.; Brat, G.
abstract: PurposeObjective assessment of open surgical skills remains limited by expert availability. Machine learning (ML)-based hand keypoint detection offers potential for automated, on-demand assessment, but performance in accessible browser-based recording environments (laptop-webcam video recorded in a web browser) is unknown. We hypothesized that browser-based recordings would achieve acceptable keypoint localization (percentage of correct keypoints [PCK] >70%). MethodsRetrospective technical validation of prospectively collected video from 14 PGY-1 interns at one academic center (July to August 2024). We annotated 203 frames (101 browser-based, 1280x720/854x480; 102 overhead, 3840x2160/1920x1080), yielding 6,232 ground-truth keypoints. An internally developed pipeline and MediaPipe Hands were evaluated. The primary endpoint was PCK normalized to the index-proximal bone; bounding-box-normalized PCK, detection rate, and per-region accuracy were also evaluated. ResultsPrimary PCK, normalized to a fixed anatomical hand scale, was 85.9% (95% CI, 80.3-91.0) for browser-based recordings and 81.5% (95% CI, 76.7-87.0) for overhead recordings. Secondary bounding-box-normalized PCK showed a similar pattern (91.6% vs 90.6%), and detection rates were high in both environments (94.9% vs 97.7%). In contrast, MediaPipe detection rates were only 5.3% for browser-based recordings and 15.4% for overhead recordings, resulting in substantially lower accuracy. ConclusionHand keypoint detection performance was comparable between browser-based and overhead recordings using the internally developed pipeline. These findings suggest that browser-based video acquisition can provide data of sufficient quality for ML-based hand keypoint detection, offering a scalable pathway for surgical skill assessment without specialized recording hardware.

infographic.key_insight: An internally developed hand-keypoint detection pipeline achieved 85.9% accuracy on browser-recorded surgical training videos versus 81.5% on overhead recordings.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Browser-based video could make automated surgical skill assessment more accessible without specialized recording hardware, though skill-assessment validity was not established.
method: Retrospective technical validation of videos from 14 PGY-1 interns at one academic center.
Annotated 203 frames with 6,232 ground-truth hand keypoints across browser-based and overhead recordings.
Compared an internal pipeline with MediaPipe Hands using keypoint localization accuracy and detection rates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Anatomically normalized percentage of correct keypoints was 85.9% (95% CI, 80.3–91.0) for browser recordings and 81.5% (76.7–87.0) for overhead recordings; internal-pipeline detection rates were 94.9% and 97.7%, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: The small, single-center technical validation does not establish generalizability or demonstrate accurate assessment of surgical skill.
infographic.paper_title: Browser-Based Video Supports Scalable Computer Vision Analysis for Open Surgical Skill Assessment

title: BioLT: Streaming Biosignal Modeling
authors: Han, J.; Liu, Y.; Tang, W.; Thwaites, L.; Clifton, D. A.; Gu, X.
abstract: AO_SCPLOWBSTRACTC_SCPLOWClinical biosignals such as ECG, PPG, and EEG are increasingly acquired as hours-long streams from bedside monitors and wearables, yet existing analysis pipelines almost universally operate on isolated short windows of around 10 seconds and cannot process the long, irregular, frequently interrupted signals. We introduce BioLT, a streaming decoder-only framework for long-context biosignal modeling that turns any window-level feature extractor or pretrained biosignal foundation model into a streaming model. BioLT combines (i) a discontinuity-aware encoding that exposes the inter-window elapsed time as an explicit input channel, so that the decoder can learn to model these gaps as clinically meaningful information, and (ii) a fixed-size compressed memory bank supervised with cumulative summary statistics, which keeps both training and inference linear in the recording length while preserving long-range context. We evaluate on CPSC-2021, VitalDB, MC-MED, and CHB-MIT for arrhythmia, sepsis, and seizure detection and for forecasting up to 20 minutes ahead, using domain features and embeddings from six biosignal foundation models. Across 21 dataset-feature settings, BioLT achieves the highest detection AUROC in 15 and the highest 20-minute forecasting AUROC in 13 settings, and shows consistent performance gains over state-of-the-art snapshot foundation-model embeddings. These highlight the importance of modeling how streaming biosignal representations evolve over time, beyond improving window-level representations alone.

infographic.key_insight: BioLT extends window-level biosignal models to long, interrupted streams by tracking time gaps and compressing prior context into a fixed-size memory.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could support continuous ECG, PPG, and EEG analysis for arrhythmia, sepsis, and seizure detection and forecasting up to 20 minutes ahead.
method: Wraps window-level feature extractors or pretrained biosignal models in a streaming decoder-only framework.
Encodes elapsed time between windows to account for signal interruptions.
Uses a compressed memory bank supervised by cumulative summary statistics, keeping computation linear in recording length.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across CPSC-2021, VitalDB, MC-MED, and CHB-MIT, BioLT achieved the highest detection AUROC in 15 of 21 dataset-feature settings and the highest 20-minute forecasting AUROC in 13.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish prospective clinical utility, real-world alert burden, or deployment reliability.
infographic.paper_title: BioLT: Streaming Biosignal Modeling
